lead: An op-amp is a differential amplifier with enormous gain. A few microvolts between its inputs slam the output against a supply rail. So we define an ideal op-amp — infinite gain, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance — and use it only with negative feedback. Feedback forces the two inputs to almost the same voltage (the virtual short), and the inputs draw no current. These rules turn transistor circuits into resistor arithmetic and underlie every amplifier, filter, integrator and converter in this unit.
prereq: You need: the differential pair, common-mode gain, offset, bias current and slew rate from Unit 5, and negative feedback and loop gain from Unit 4, Feedback Amplifiers and Oscillators.

sections.h3: The ideal op-amp and its five promises

blocks.text: An op-amp has two inputs and one output. The output responds only to the difference between the input voltages, not to their common value. The non-inverting input is v₊ and the inverting input v₋, both measured to ground.

blocks.where: v_d is the differential input voltage in volts; v₊ and v₋ are the input pin voltages in volts, each to ground.
v_out is the output voltage in volts; A<sub>OL</sub> is the open-loop gain, a pure number, measured with no feedback; v_d is the differential input in volts.

blocks.text: An ideal op-amp pushes five properties to their limits: infinite open-loop gain A<sub>OL</sub>; infinite input resistance R<sub>in</sub>; zero output resistance R<sub>o</sub>; infinite bandwidth, so gain and zero phase shift hold at every frequency; and zero offset, zero drift and zero bias current. Some syllabi call this the IOA model.

The model is a controlled source A<sub>OL</sub>·v_d at the output, with R<sub>in</sub> across the inputs and R<sub>o</sub> in series. Infinite R<sub>in</sub> means no current enters either pin. Zero R<sub>o</sub> means the output does not sag under load. Both keep the design equations linear, so gain is set by resistor ratios alone.

head: Property
Ideal op-amp
Practical op-amp
rows: a few Hz to tens of Hz

blocks.text: Plot v_out vertically against v_d. You get a straight line through the origin with slope A<sub>OL</sub>, and the line flattens at the supply rails. The output can never exceed the supplies, so it saturates about 1 V inside them: with ±12 V supplies the flat top sits near +11 V and the flat bottom near −11 V.
The steep straight part is the linear region, and its width is tiny.

blocks.where: V<sub>sat</sub> is the saturation output magnitude in volts, roughly supply minus 1 V; A<sub>OL</sub> is the open-loop gain, a pure number; the result is in volts and is the total span of v_d that keeps the output linear.

blocks.text: Take Vsat = 11 V and AOL = 2 × 10⁵. The strip is 22 / (2 × 10⁵) = 110 µV, that is ±55 µV. One millivolt of input is twenty times too big. So an op-amp is useless as a linear amplifier with no feedback: you cannot hold the input difference that steady. Used deliberately without feedback, the same device is a comparator giving one rail or the other, covered in 6.9.

Negative feedback changes the picture. The feedback network returns a fraction of the output to v₋, so v_d only has to supply the small difference between the input and that fraction. The operating point slides back into the steep region and stays there.
Split the output equation into its two factors.

blocks.where: v_d is the differential input in volts; v_out is the output in volts; A<sub>OL</sub> is the open-loop gain.

blocks.text: If the output is 5 V and AOL is 10⁵, v_d is only 50 µV. Per volt at the output you need just 10 µV at the input. So while the output is inside the linear range, the two inputs sit at almost the same voltage: v₊ ≈ v₋. This is the virtual short. It is a voltage condition only. The pins are not wired together, and since Rin is infinite the current between them is zero.

When v₊ is tied to ground, the rule says v₋ also sits at 0 V even though that pin is not grounded. This is the virtual ground, the engine of the inverting amplifier in 6.2, the summing amplifier in 6.3, the integrator in 6.5 and the voltage-to-current converter in 6.6.
Two conditions must both hold: negative feedback must be present, and the computed output must lie between the supply rails. Run this check first.

items: Trace a path from the output pin back to an input pin.
Confirm it returns to v₋. A path to v₊ is positive feedback and gives no virtual short.
Solve assuming v₊ = v₋ and check the answer lies inside the saturation limits.
If outside, the op-amp is saturated and v_out is fixed at the rail.
Then set both input currents to zero and solve the resistor network with Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws.

blocks.text: Break either condition and the rule dies. Positive feedback gives no virtual short, and the two thresholds are set by the resistors instead (see 6.9). A circuit whose ideal output would be 20 V on ±12 V supplies is simply saturated at +11 V, and the input difference is no longer near zero.

figure.caption: Signal path through the ideal op-amp model: the two pins form v_d, the controlled source multiplies it by the open-loop gain of 2 × 10⁵ from the worked example, and a zero output resistance drives the load without loss.

spec.title: Ideal op-amp model
spec.aria: The ideal op-amp model drawn downwards: the two inputs form v_d, a controlled source multiplies it by the open-loop gain of 2 times 10 to the 5, and a zero output resistance feeds v_out.

examples.question: An op-amp has an open-loop gain A<sub>OL</sub> = 2 × 10⁵ and runs on ±12 V supplies, saturating about 1 V inside each rail. (a) Find the output for v_d = 100 µV. (b) Find the largest v_d that still keeps the amplifier in its linear region.
steps: Convert the input to volts: v_d = 100 µV = 100 × 10⁻⁶ V = 1 × 10⁻⁴ V.
Apply the open-loop law: v_out = A<sub>OL</sub> · v_d = (2 × 10⁵) × (1 × 10⁻⁴) = 20 V.
The rails are ±12 V, so the output cannot pass about +11 V.
20 V > 11 V, so the amplifier saturates. The actual output is v_out = +11 V, not 20 V.
For (b), the edge of the linear region is where A<sub>OL</sub> · v_d,max = V<sub>sat</sub>.
So v_d,max = V<sub>sat</sub> / A<sub>OL</sub> = 11 / (2 × 10⁵) = 5.5 × 10⁻⁵ V = 55 µV.
The full linear strip is twice this, 110 µV wide. Any differential input larger than 55 µV drives this op-amp into saturation when it is used open loop.
examples.answer: For v_d = 100 µV the ideal output is 20 V, so the amplifier saturates at about +11 V; the largest input that keeps it linear is 55 µV.

traps: Writing v₊ = v₋ for an open-loop or positive-feedback circuit. The virtual short holds only while negative feedback keeps the output inside the linear range.
Treating the virtual short as a wire. No current flows between the input pins, but the resistor currents around them are certainly not zero.
Reporting the ideal output when it is beyond the rails. A computed 20 V on ±12 V supplies must be corrected to about +11 V.
Unit slips between microvolts and volts: 100 µV is 1 × 10⁻⁴ V, not 1 × 10⁻⁶ V. A factor of 100 in v_d becomes a factor of 100 in v_out.
Assuming ideal infinite bandwidth means the real gain stays at A<sub>OL</sub> at every frequency. Open-loop gain rolls off with frequency, as covered in Unit 3.

quiz.q: List the five ideal properties of an op-amp.
quiz.a: Infinite open-loop gain, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance, infinite bandwidth, and zero offset, drift and bias current.

quiz.q: Define virtual ground in one sentence.
quiz.a: When v₊ is held at ground and negative feedback keeps the output linear, the inverting input v₋ sits at almost 0 V without any physical connection to ground.

quiz.q: Why does negative feedback produce a virtual short?
quiz.a: Because v_d = v_out / A<sub>OL</sub>. With A<sub>OL</sub> near 10⁵, a few volts at the output need only tens of microvolts at the input, so v₊ and v₋ differ by an amount small enough to treat as zero.

quiz.q: Why is the open-loop linear strip so narrow, and what follows for linear amplification?
quiz.a: Its width is 2V<sub>sat</sub>/A<sub>OL</sub>, so a huge gain shrinks it; with V<sub>sat</sub> = 11 V and A<sub>OL</sub> = 2 × 10⁵ it is only 110 µV. No real source can be held that steady, so open-loop linear amplification is impossible and negative feedback is required.

quiz.q: An op-amp has A<sub>OL</sub> = 10⁵ and ±15 V supplies, saturating 1 V inside the rails. Find the maximum differential input for linear operation and the ideal output for v_d = −40 µV.
quiz.a: V<sub>sat</sub> = 15 − 1 = 14 V. v_d,max = 14 / 10⁵ = 140 µV. For v_d = −40 µV, v_out = 10⁵ × (−40 × 10⁻⁶) = −4 V, inside ±14 V, so the output is −4 V and the amplifier stays linear.

quiz.q: A student analyses a negative-feedback circuit with A<sub>OL</sub> = 10⁵ and ±12 V supplies and concludes v₊ = v₋ = 0.2 V. Is that trustworthy?
quiz.a: Check the implied output first. The conclusion holds only if the solved output lies inside ±11 V. If the ideal solution gives, say, 30 V, the op-amp is saturated, the virtual short has failed, and the real output is pinned near +11 V.

quiz.q: A comparator and an inverting amplifier use the same op-amp. Why does the virtual short apply to one and not the other?
quiz.a: The inverting amplifier returns a fraction of the output to v₋, which is negative feedback, so v₊ = v₋ holds. The comparator has no feedback path, so v_d is free and the output sits at one rail or the other. The device is identical; only the connection differs.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real design starts where the ideal model stops: offset voltage becomes a systematic error that must be trimmed or auto-zeroed, and bias current turns into an offset through your feedback resistors. Chopper-stabilised and zero-drift op-amps cancel offset continuously, which is why they suit medical instrumentation and load-cell weighing. The same ideal rules apply to the operational transconductance amplifier, whose output is a current g_m·v_d, and to fully differential op-amps with a common-mode feedback loop.
